## Overview

The Mon are an ethnic group inhabiting Lower Myanmar’s Mon State, Kayin State, Kayah State, Tanintharyi Region, Bago Region and the Irrawaddy Delta, as well as several areas of Thailand. In Myanmar, the Mon are a major ethnic group; in Thailand, they are a minor ethnic group. The 2007 estimate for Mon speakers was between 1,800,000 and 2 million, while the number of Mon speakers in Thailand was estimated at between 60,000 and 80,000. The Mon language belongs to the Monic group of the Austroasiatic family and is closely related to Nyah Kur. The Mon were among the earliest peoples of Mainland Southeast Asia and established early states including Dvaravati, Hariphunchai and Thaton. They also played a major role in the spread of Theravada Buddhism and influenced the scripts, languages and cultures of neighboring societies.

## Material culture

### Architecture

Mon communities built their own Buddhist temples in Thailand. The sources also state that Burmese vocabulary borrowed from Mon is especially associated with administration, architecture, cloth, cuisine and flowers. No specific Mon house form, roof type, construction material, temple plan, or architectural ornament is described.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources mention an amulet-type object from Chan Sen in Nakhon Sawan province, dating to the 6th century and inscribed in Old Mon on the obverse. They also mention votive images from Saraphi district, now in the National Museum, Lopburi, and votive tablets from Mueang Fa Daet. No broader account of Mon ceramics, metalwork, woodworking, tools, or household goods is provided.

## Music & performance

The sources identify the *Mahagita*, the corpus of Burmese classical songs, as containing an eponymous song genre associated with the historical term “Talaing.” The term was used for the Mon during the pre-colonial and colonial periods, and its use survives in fixed historical expressions including this song genre.

The Mon language itself has an important place in regional textual culture. Old Mon Jātaka glosses from the 11th and 12th centuries are documented at Pagan, including on the Ananda plaques, at West Taungbi and on the west wall of the Lokahteikpan. The sources describe these glosses as naming the Jātaka and then the Bodhisatta. They also mention Thai glosses on Jātaka slabs at Wat Si Chum as following the same pattern.

## Festivals & rituals

Mon National Day was established in 1947 to commemorate the founding of Hanthawady, described as the last Mon Kingdom centered in Pegu. The holiday is observed on the full moon of the 11th month of the Mon lunar calendar. In Phrapadaeng, Thailand, it coincides with the Songkran festival.

The Mon were among the first peoples in Mainland Southeast Asia to receive Theravada Buddhist missionaries from Sri Lanka. Mon communities built Buddhist temples, and the Mon kingdoms of Dvaravati, Hariphunchai and Thaton are associated in the sources with the early spread of Theravada Buddhism.

The sources describe historical migration, political conflict and religious continuity rather than a full annual ritual calendar. They record that the Mon of Siam maintained contact with Lower Burma through pilgrimage, trade and monastic networks.

## Foodways

 They state only that Burmese has borrowed vocabulary from Mon in areas including cuisine and flowers.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources refer to Bamar and Lanna chronicles in connection with the Thaton Kingdom, whose remains have not been found but which is widely mentioned in those chronicles. They also refer to the Northern Thai Chronicles and the Northern Thai Chronicle *Cāmadevivaṃsa* in accounts of Lavo, Queen Camadevi and the foundation of Hariphunchai and Khelang Nakhon.

Mon historical writing is also represented by inscriptions. The ethnonym “rmeñ” was first recorded in Kyanzittha’s New Palace Inscription of AD 1102 in Myanmar. The Myazedi inscription contains the same story in Pali, Pyu, Mon and Burmese on its four sides. Old Mon Jātaka glosses are documented at Pagan, and inscriptions from Thailand include texts connected with votive images, tablets and Jātaka scenes.

## Language & religion

Mon is an Austroasiatic language in the Monic group, closely related to Nyah Kur and more distantly related to Khmer and Vietnamese. It is not tonal. Instead, it has a vowel-phonation or vowel-register system with clear and breathy voice. Mon nouns do not inflect for singular and plural, verbs do not inflect for person, tense is shown through particles, adjectives follow the noun, and the ordinary sentence order is subject–verb–object.

The principal Burmese dialects are Central, Bago and Ye, and the sources describe them as mutually intelligible. The Mon of Myanmar are also classified as Mon Nya, Mon Tang and Mon Teh according to ancestral region. The writing system is based on Indic scripts. The Mon adopted the Pallava script, and the oldest form of the Mon script was discovered in a cave in modern-day Saraburi, dating to around 550 CE. The Tai Tham alphabet and Burmese alphabet are described as adaptations of the Mon script.

The Mon were important in the spread of Theravada Buddhism in Mainland Southeast Asia. Mon was classified as a “vulnerable” language in UNESCO’s 2010 *Atlas of the World’s Languages in Danger*, and Mon-language use has declined particularly among younger speakers in Myanmar and Thailand.
